claim: Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) infection is associated with rheumatoid arthritis (RA) in adults.
source: Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) infection is associated with rheumatoid arthritis (RA) in adults, though the nature of the relationship remains unknown.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to existing literature establishing the association between EBV and RA.

claim: The nature of the relationship between EBV infection and RA remains unknown.
source: Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) infection is associated with rheumatoid arthritis (RA) in adults, though the nature of the relationship remains unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Latent gammaherpesvirus infection enhances clinical arthritis in mice.
source: We have provided the first evidence that latent gammaherpesvirus infection enhances clinical arthritis, modeling EBV's role in RA.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Mice latently infected with gammaherpesvirus 68 (γHV68) develop more severe collagen-induced arthritis.
source: Mice latently infected with a murine analog of EBV, gammaherpesvirus 68 (γHV68), develop more severe collagen-induced arthritis and a Th1-skewed immune profile reminiscent of human disease.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Mice latently infected with γHV68 develop a Th1-skewed immune profile reminiscent of human disease.
source: Mice latently infected with a murine analog of EBV, gammaherpesvirus 68 (γHV68), develop more severe collagen-induced arthritis and a Th1-skewed immune profile reminiscent of human disease.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data on T cell phenotypes and cytokine expression.

claim: Disease enhancement by γHV68 requires viral latency and is not due to active virus stimulation of the immune response.
source: We demonstrate that disease enhancement requires viral latency and is not due to active virus stimulation of the immune response.
evidence: This is supported by experiments using ACRTA-γHV68, a virus that does not establish latency.

claim: Age-associated B cells (ABCs) are associated with several human autoimmune diseases, including arthritis.
source: Age-associated B cells (ABCs) are associated with several human autoimmune diseases, including arthritis, though their contribution to disease is not well understood.
evidence: This is supported by citations to existing literature on ABCs in autoimmune diseases.

claim: The contribution of ABCs to disease is not well understood.
source: Age-associated B cells (ABCs) are associated with several human autoimmune diseases, including arthritis, though their contribution to disease is not well understood.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: ABCs are mechanistically required for viral enhancement of arthritis disease.
source: Using ABC knockout mice, we have provided the first evidence that ABCs are mechanistically required for viral enhancement of disease, thereby establishing that ABCs are impacted by latent gammaherpesvirus infection and provoke arthritis.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experiments using ABC knockout mice shown in Figure 6.

claim: ABCs are impacted by latent gammaherpesvirus infection.
source: Using ABC knockout mice, we have provided the first evidence that ABCs are mechanistically required for viral enhancement of disease, thereby establishing that ABCs are impacted by latent gammaherpesvirus infection and provoke arthritis.
evidence: This is supported by data showing changes in ABC phenotype and numbers during γHV68-CIA.

claim: ABCs provoke arthritis in the context of latent gammaherpesvirus infection.
source: Using ABC knockout mice, we have provided the first evidence that ABCs are mechanistically required for viral enhancement of disease, thereby establishing that ABCs are impacted by latent gammaherpesvirus infection and provoke arthritis.
evidence: This is supported by data showing that ABC knockout mice do not develop enhanced arthritis with γHV68 infection.

claim: RA is one of the most common autoimmune diseases in adults.
source: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is one of the most common autoimmune diseases in adults, though the etiology and pathophysiology are not fully understood (Humphreys et al., 2013; Firestein and McInnes, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to existing literature on RA epidemiology.

claim: The etiology and pathophysiology of RA are not fully understood.
source: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is one of the most common autoimmune diseases in adults, though the etiology and pathophysiology are not fully understood (Humphreys et al., 2013; Firestein and McInnes, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to existing literature and represents current state of knowledge.

claim: RA is associated with Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) infection.
source: RA, as well as other autoimmune diseases including multiple sclerosis (MS) and systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), is associated with Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) infection (Balandraud et al., 2003; Ascherio and Munger, 2007; Gross et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to existing literature.

claim: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is associated with Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) infection.
source: RA, as well as other autoimmune diseases including multiple sclerosis (MS) and systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), is associated with Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) infection (Balandraud et al., 2003; Ascherio and Munger, 2007; Gross et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to existing literature.

claim: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is associated with Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) infection.
source: RA, as well as other autoimmune diseases including multiple sclerosis (MS) and systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), is associated with Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) infection (Balandraud et al., 2003; Ascherio and Munger, 2007; Gross et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to existing literature.

claim: EBV infection typically takes place during childhood or adolescence.
source: EBV infection typically takes place during childhood or adolescence, while RA generally becomes symptomatic during middle age, indicating that the latent EBV infection likely modulates the immune system over time in a manner that contributes to the development of RA (Humphreys et al., 2013; Dowd et al., 2013; Fourcade et al., 2017; Alamanos et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to existing literature on EBV infection timing.

claim: RA generally becomes symptomatic during middle age.
source: EBV infection typically takes place during childhood or adolescence, while RA generally becomes symptomatic during middle age, indicating that the latent EBV infection likely modulates the immune system over time in a manner that contributes to the development of RA (Humphreys et al., 2013; Dowd et al., 2013; Fourcade et al., 2017; Alamanos et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to existing literature on RA onset.

claim: Latent EBV infection likely modulates the immune system over time in a manner that contributes to the development of RA.
source: EBV infection typically takes place during childhood or adolescence, while RA generally becomes symptomatic during middle age, indicating that the latent EBV infection likely modulates the immune system over time in a manner that contributes to the development of RA (Humphreys et al., 2013; Dowd et al., 2013; Fourcade et al., 2017; Alamanos et al., 2006).
evidence: This is an inference based on the temporal relationship between EBV infection and RA onset, supported by citations.

claim: The circulating EBV load is higher in individuals with RA than in otherwise healthy adults.
source: The circulating EBV load is higher in individuals with RA than in otherwise healthy adults (Balandraud et al., 2003), and RA patients have increased levels of antibodies specific to multiple EBV-encoded proteins (Blaschke et al., 2000; Ferrell et al., 1981; Catalano et al., 1979; Alspaugh et al., 1981; Hazelton et al., 1987).
evidence: This is supported by citation to existing literature.

claim: RA patients have increased levels of antibodies specific to multiple EBV-encoded proteins.
source: The circulating EBV load is higher in individuals with RA than in otherwise healthy adults (Balandraud et al., 2003), and RA patients have increased levels of antibodies specific to multiple EBV-encoded proteins (Blaschke et al., 2000; Ferrell et al., 1981; Catalano et al., 1979; Alspaugh et al., 1981; Hazelton et al., 1987).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to existing literature.

claim: RA patients have increased EBV-specific CD8+ T cells.
source: Further, RA patients have increased EBV-specific CD8+ T cells (Lünemann et al., 2008), yet these cells have a reduced ability to kill EBV-infected B cells when compared to the same subset of EBV-specific CD8+ T cells from healthy controls (Takei et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to existing literature.

claim: EBV-specific CD8+ T cells from RA patients have a reduced ability to kill EBV-infected B cells when compared to the same subset from healthy controls.
source: Further, RA patients have increased EBV-specific CD8+ T cells (Lünemann et al., 2008), yet these cells have a reduced ability to kill EBV-infected B cells when compared to the same subset of EBV-specific CD8+ T cells from healthy controls (Takei et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to existing literature.

claim: The precise role of EBV in RA pathogenesis remains unknown.
source: However, the precise role of EBV in RA pathogenesis remains unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Evidence from in vivo models examining EBV's role in RA is scarce.
source: Evidence from in vivo models is scarce and previous studies have focused primarily on the direct relationship between EBV infection and damage to the joint capsule, with little attention given to systemic effects of EBV infection on immune modulation preceding and continuing throughout disease (Kuwana et al., 2011; LeBel et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of research in the field, supported by citations.

claim: Previous studies have focused primarily on the direct relationship between EBV infection and damage to the joint capsule.
source: Evidence from in vivo models is scarce and previous studies have focused primarily on the direct relationship between EBV infection and damage to the joint capsule, with little attention given to systemic effects of EBV infection on immune modulation preceding and continuing throughout disease (Kuwana et al., 2011; LeBel et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to existing literature.

claim: Little attention has been given to systemic effects of EBV infection on immune modulation preceding and continuing throughout disease.
source: Evidence from in vivo models is scarce and previous studies have focused primarily on the direct relationship between EBV infection and damage to the joint capsule, with little attention given to systemic effects of EBV infection on immune modulation preceding and continuing throughout disease (Kuwana et al., 2011; LeBel et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of research in the field, supported by citations.

claim: Mice with humanized immune systems infected with EBV spontaneously develop erosive arthritis.
source: Mice with humanized immune systems, namely NOD/Shi-scid/IL-2Rγnull mice reconstituted with CD34+ hematopoietic stem cells, that were infected with EBV went on to spontaneously develop erosive arthritis, suggesting a causative role of EBV in arthritis development (Kuwana et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to existing literature.

claim: Ly6Chigh monocytes play a role in transporting murine gammaherpesvirus 68 (γHV68) to the synovium.
source: Related, a serum transfer‐induced arthritis model was used to demonstrate that Ly6Chigh monocytes play a role in transporting murine gammaherpesvirus 68 (γHV68), an EBV homolog, to the synovium (LeBel et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to existing literature.

claim: Latent γHV68 infection exacerbates experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE).
source: Our group has previously shown that latent γHV68 infection exacerbates experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE) and leads to a disease that more closely resembles MS, with increased demyelination and infiltration of CD8 to cells of the central nervous system in γHV68-infected mice (Casiraghi et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Latent γHV68 infection leads to a disease that more closely resembles MS, with increased demyelination and infiltration of CD8 cells to the central nervous system.
source: Our group has previously shown that latent γHV68 infection exacerbates experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE) and leads to a disease that more closely resembles MS, with increased demyelination and infiltration of CD8 to cells of the central nervous system in γHV68-infected mice (Casiraghi et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: The enhancement of EAE by γHV68 is specific to γHV68; other viruses, including LCMV and MCMV, do not lead to enhancement of EAE.
source: Critically, this enhancement was specific to γHV68; other viruses, including lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus (LCMV) and murine cytomegalovirus (MCMV), did not lead to enhancement of EAE.
evidence: This is supported by inference from previous work by the authors.

claim: Enhancement of EAE by γHV68 takes place without changes to autoantibody levels.
source: Additionally, enhancement took place without changes to autoantibody levels.
evidence: This is supported by inference from previous work by the authors.

claim: γHV68 is a natural pathogen that is a well-established and widely-used murine model of EBV infection.
source: γHV68 is a natural pathogen that is a well-established and widely-used murine model of EBV infection that shares an array of characteristics with human EBV infection, including latent persistence in B cells, viral reactivation from latency, a potent CD8 T cell response, and immune evasion tactics (Olivadoti et al., 2007; Wirtz et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to existing literature on γHV68 as a model system.

claim: γHV68 shares an array of characteristics with human EBV infection, including latent persistence in B cells, viral reactivation from latency, a potent CD8 T cell response, and immune evasion tactics.
source: γHV68 is a natural pathogen that is a well-established and widely-used murine model of EBV infection that shares an array of characteristics with human EBV infection, including latent persistence in B cells, viral reactivation from latency, a potent CD8 T cell response, and immune evasion tactics (Olivadoti et al., 2007; Wirtz et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to existing literature on γHV68 characteristics.

claim: Type II collagen-induced arthritis (CIA) is a commonly used model of RA.
source: Type II collagen-induced arthritis (CIA) is a commonly used model of RA wherein mice are injected with type II collagen emulsified in an adjuvant.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the CIA model.

claim: Multiple strains of mice are susceptible to CIA, including C57BL/6 mice.
source: Multiple strains of mice are susceptible to CIA, including C57BL/6 mice that, despite displaying a less severe disease course than other strains, generate a robust T cell response (Inglis et al., 2007; Campbell et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to existing literature on CIA susceptibility.

claim: C57BL/6 mice display a less severe CIA disease course than other strains but generate a robust T cell response.
source: Multiple strains of mice are susceptible to CIA, including C57BL/6 mice that, despite displaying a less severe disease course than other strains, generate a robust T cell response (Inglis et al., 2007; Campbell et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to existing literature on C57BL/6 CIA characteristics.

claim: In C57BL/6 mice, CIA follows a chronic disease course with a sustained T cell response, presence of anti-collagen IgG, and infiltration of inflammatory lymphocytes into the joint capsule.
source: In C57BL/6 mice, CIA follows a chronic disease course with a sustained T cell response, presence of anti-collagen IgG, and infiltration of inflammatory lymphocytes into the joint capsule (Inglis et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to existing literature on C57BL/6 CIA characteristics.

claim: EBV primary infection generally takes place in childhood or adolescence.
source: EBV primary infection generally takes place in childhood or adolescence (Dowd et al., 2013; Fourcade et al., 2017), and RA can occur at any age, though the mean incidence is in the sixth decade of life (Myasoedova et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to existing literature on EBV infection timing.

claim: RA can occur at any age, though the mean incidence is in the sixth decade of life.
source: EBV primary infection generally takes place in childhood or adolescence (Dowd et al., 2013; Fourcade et al., 2017), and RA can occur at any age, though the mean incidence is in the sixth decade of life (Myasoedova et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to existing literature on RA incidence.

claim: C57BL/6J mice infected with latent γHV68 and induced for CIA develop a more severe clinical course compared to uninfected CIA controls.
source: Here we have shown that C57BL/6J mice infected with latent γHV68 and induced for CIA develop a more severe clinical course and an altered immunological profile compared to uninfected CIA controls, with expanded CD8+ T cells and Th1 skewing.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: C57BL/6J mice infected with latent γHV68 and induced for CIA develop an altered immunological profile compared to uninfected CIA controls, with expanded CD8+ T cells and Th1 skewing.
source: Here we have shown that C57BL/6J mice infected with latent γHV68 and induced for CIA develop a more severe clinical course and an altered immunological profile compared to uninfected CIA controls, with expanded CD8+ T cells and Th1 skewing.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: B cells contribute pathogenically to RA.
source: The role of B cells in the relationship between EBV and RA is intriguing because B cells contribute pathogenically to RA, and EBV infects B cells and alters the B cell profile (Marston et al., 2010; Hatton et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to existing literature on B cells in RA.

claim: EBV infects B cells and alters the B cell profile.
source: The role of B cells in the relationship between EBV and RA is intriguing because B cells contribute pathogenically to RA, and EBV infects B cells and alters the B cell profile (Marston et al., 2010; Hatton et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to existing literature on EBV and B cells.

claim: The relative proportion and/or absolute circulating counts of ABCs are elevated in RA patients compared to healthy adults.
source: When compared to healthy adults, the relative proportion and/or absolute circulating counts of ABCs are elevated in RA patients, a subset of individuals with MS, individuals with SLE, and a subset of people with common variable immune deficiency that displays autoimmune complications (Adlowitz et al., 2015; Rubtsov et al., 2011; Thorarinsdottir et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2019; Claes et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2019; Rakhmanov et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to existing literature on ABCs in RA.

claim: The relative proportion and/or absolute circulating counts of ABCs are elevated in a subset of individuals with MS compared to healthy adults.
source: When compared to healthy adults, the relative proportion and/or absolute circulating counts of ABCs are elevated in RA patients, a subset of individuals with MS, individuals with SLE, and a subset of people with common variable immune deficiency that displays autoimmune complications (Adlowitz et al., 2015; Rubtsov et al., 2011; Thorarinsdottir et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2019; Claes et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2019; Rakhmanov et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to existing literature on ABCs in MS.

claim: The relative proportion and/or absolute circulating counts of ABCs are elevated in individuals with SLE compared to healthy adults.
source: When compared to healthy adults, the relative proportion and/or absolute circulating counts of ABCs are elevated in RA patients, a subset of individuals with MS, individuals with SLE, and a subset of people with common variable immune deficiency that displays autoimmune complications (Adlowitz et al., 2015; Rubtsov et al., 2011; Thorarinsdottir et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2019; Claes et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2019; Rakhmanov et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to existing literature on ABCs in SLE.

claim: The relative proportion and/or absolute circulating counts of ABCs are elevated in a subset of people with common variable immune deficiency that displays autoimmune complications compared to healthy adults.
source: When compared to healthy adults, the relative proportion and/or absolute circulating counts of ABCs are elevated in RA patients, a subset of individuals with MS, individuals with SLE, and a subset of people with common variable immune deficiency that displays autoimmune complications (Adlowitz et al., 2015; Rubtsov et al., 2011; Thorarinsdottir et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2019; Claes et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2019; Rakhmanov et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to existing literature on ABCs in immune deficiency.

claim: ABCs are required for disease development in mouse models of SLE.
source: ABCs are required for disease development in mouse models of SLE (Rubtsova et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to existing literature on ABCs in SLE models.

claim: ABCs are increased during viral infections in mice and/or humans including LCMV, γHV68, vaccinia, hepatitis C virus, HIV, and influenza.
source: Also, ABCs are increased during viral infections in mice and/or humans including LCMV, γHV68, vaccinia, hepatitis C virus, HIV, and influenza (Rubtsova et al., 2013; Chang et al., 2017; Knox et al., 2017; Johnson et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to existing literature on ABCs in viral infections.

claim: ABCs display an array of functional capacities, including the secretion of anti-viral or autoantibodies, initiation of germinal centers, antigen presentation to T cells, and secretion of cytokines.
source: ABCs display an array of functional capacities, including the secretion of anti-viral or autoantibodies, initiation of germinal centers, antigen presentation to T cells, and secretion of cytokines (Rubtsova et al., 2013; Chang et al., 2017; Knox et al., 2017; Johnson et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to existing literature on ABC functions.

claim: ABC KO mice are unable to develop the γHV68-exacerbation of CIA.
source: We found that ABC KO mice are unable to develop the γHV68-exacerbation of CIA and therefore act as a mediator between viral infection and autoimmunity.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: ABCs act as a mediator between viral infection and autoimmunity.
source: We found that ABC KO mice are unable to develop the γHV68-exacerbation of CIA and therefore act as a mediator between viral infection and autoimmunity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing that ABC knockout prevents γHV68-exacerbation of CIA.

claim: CIA in latent γHV68-infected mice had a more severe clinical course than uninfected mice, as evidenced by consistently higher clinical scores and changes in paw heights throughout the clinical course.
source: We observed that CIA in latent γHV68-infected mice (herein referred to as γHV68-CIA mice) had a more severe clinical course than uninfected mice (herein referred to as CIA mice), as evidenced by consistently higher clinical scores and changes in paw heights throughout the clinical course (Figure 1A–B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A-B.

claim: γHV68-CIA mice developed onset of disease symptoms an average of 7 days earlier than CIA mice.
source: γHV68-CIA mice also developed onset of disease symptoms an average of 7 days earlier than CIA mice, reached a higher score at endpoint, and displayed a higher cumulative score (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C-D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: γHV68-CIA mice reached a higher score at endpoint than CIA mice.
source: γHV68-CIA mice also developed onset of disease symptoms an average of 7 days earlier than CIA mice, reached a higher score at endpoint, and displayed a higher cumulative score (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C-D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: γHV68-CIA mice displayed a higher cumulative score than CIA mice.
source: γHV68-CIA mice also developed onset of disease symptoms an average of 7 days earlier than CIA mice, reached a higher score at endpoint, and displayed a higher cumulative score (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C-D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Male and female mice displayed similar clinical scores during CIA.
source: In agreement with other research groups (Campbell et al., 2000), male and female mice displayed similar clinical scores during CIA, and we also did not observe a sex difference in γHV68-CIA mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E and citation to existing literature.

claim: There was no sex difference in clinical scores in γHV68-CIA mice.
source: In agreement with other research groups (Campbell et al., 2000), male and female mice displayed similar clinical scores during CIA, and we also did not observe a sex difference in γHV68-CIA mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Titers of anti-type II collagen autoantibodies (total IgG, IgG1, and IgG2c) were elevated in sera from mice with CIA compared to naive mice without CIA.
source: Titers of anti-type II collagen autoantibodies (total IgG, IgG1, and IgG2c) were elevated in sera from mice with CIA compared to naive mice without CIA, yet were similar in mice with CIA regardless of infection (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F–H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F-H.

claim: Titers of anti-type II collagen autoantibodies were similar in mice with CIA regardless of γHV68 infection.
source: Titers of anti-type II collagen autoantibodies (total IgG, IgG1, and IgG2c) were elevated in sera from mice with CIA compared to naive mice without CIA, yet were similar in mice with CIA regardless of infection (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F–H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F-H.

claim: Inducing CIA in γHV68-infected mice did not impact viral load.
source: Additionally, we found that inducing CIA in γHV68-infected mice did not impact viral load (Figure 1—figure supplement 1I), indicating that γHV68 is not reactivating.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1I.

claim: γHV68 is not reactivating during CIA.
source: Additionally, we found that inducing CIA in γHV68-infected mice did not impact viral load (Figure 1—figure supplement 1I), indicating that γHV68 is not reactivating.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that viral load does not change during CIA.

claim: Latent γHV68 infection leads to earlier onset and more severe CIA.
source: These data demonstrate that latent γHV68 infection leads to earlier onset and more severe CIA, though the exacerbation is not due to higher titers of autoantibodies against type II collagen or changes in abundance of particular immunoglobulin isotypes.
evidence: This is a summary of experimental findings from Figure 1.

claim: The exacerbation of CIA by γHV68 is not due to higher titers of autoantibodies against type II collagen or changes in abundance of particular immunoglobulin isotypes.
source: These data demonstrate that latent γHV68 infection leads to earlier onset and more severe CIA, though the exacerbation is not due to higher titers of autoantibodies against type II collagen or changes in abundance of particular immunoglobulin isotypes.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing no difference in autoantibody titers.

claim: The number of CD8+ T cells infiltrating the synovium during γHV68-CIA was increased compared to CIA (3.6-fold change).
source: The number of CD8+ T cells infiltrating the synovium during γHV68-CIA was increased compared to CIA (3.6-fold change), while there was no significant difference in the number of CD4+ T cells (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: There was no significant difference in the number of CD4+ T cells infiltrating the synovium between γHV68-CIA and CIA.
source: The number of CD8+ T cells infiltrating the synovium during γHV68-CIA was increased compared to CIA (3.6-fold change), while there was no significant difference in the number of CD4+ T cells (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: CD8+ and CD4+ T cells in γHV68-CIA synovium displayed a significant increase in Tbet expression compared to those in CIA.
source: Additionally, the CD8+ and CD4+ T cells in γHV68-CIA synovium displayed a significant increase in Tbet expression compared to those in CIA (Figure 2B), indicating Th1 skewing.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Increased Tbet expression in synovial T cells indicates Th1 skewing.
source: Additionally, the CD8+ and CD4+ T cells in γHV68-CIA synovium displayed a significant increase in Tbet expression compared to those in CIA (Figure 2B), indicating Th1 skewing.
evidence: This is an inference based on established knowledge that Tbet is a marker of Th1 cells.

claim: The relative expression of Ifng in synovium cells of γHV68-CIA mice compared to CIA mice was increased (129-fold change).
source: The relative expression of Ifng in synovium cells of γHV68-CIA mice compared to CIA mice was increased (129-fold change), while the relative expression of Il17a was trending down in infected mice (Figure 2C; 3.8-fold change), though the sample size was low due to the difficulty of obtaining these samples.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The relative expression of Il17a in synovium cells was trending down in γHV68-CIA mice compared to CIA mice (3.8-fold change).
source: The relative expression of Ifng in synovium cells of γHV68-CIA mice compared to CIA mice was increased (129-fold change), while the relative expression of Il17a was trending down in infected mice (Figure 2C; 3.8-fold change), though the sample size was low due to the difficulty of obtaining these samples.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C, though the authors note the sample size was low.

claim: IFNγ-producing T cells were preferentially infiltrating the synovium in γHV68-CIA, which is consistent with what was observed in the synovium of RA patients.
source: Together, these results indicate that IFNγ-producing T cells were preferentially infiltrating the synovium in our model of γHV68-CIA, which is consistent with what was observed in the synovium of RA patients (Yamada et al., 2008).
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data and supported by citation to existing literature on RA.

claim: There is a skewing toward cytotoxic CD8+ T cells in mice latently infected with γHV68 prior to CIA.
source: Our data also demonstrate a skewing toward cytotoxic CD8+ T cells in mice latently infected with γHV68 prior to CIA.
evidence: This is a summary of experimental findings from Figure 2.

claim: Latent γHV68 infection expands cytotoxic T cells and reduces Tregs.
source: It is known that latent γHV68 infection expands cytotoxic T cells and reduces Tregs (Casiraghi et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Cytotoxic T cells are crucial mediators of CIA.
source: Both cell types play a role in CIA with cytotoxic T cells being crucial mediators of CIA while Tregs play a protective role (Tada et al., 1996; Morgan et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to existing literature on T cells in CIA.

claim: Tregs play a protective role in CIA.
source: Both cell types play a role in CIA with cytotoxic T cells being crucial mediators of CIA while Tregs play a protective role (Tada et al., 1996; Morgan et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to existing literature on T cells in CIA.

claim: γHV68-CIA mice displayed a decrease in relative proportion of FoxP3+ Tregs in the spleen compared to control CIA mice.
source: γHV68-CIA mice displayed a decrease in relative proportion of FoxP3+ Tregs and an increase in relative proportion of CD8+ T cells in the spleen compared to control CIA mice (Figure 3A–B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, B-C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A-B.

claim: γHV68-CIA mice displayed an increase in relative proportion of CD8+ T cells in the spleen compared to control CIA mice.
source: γHV68-CIA mice displayed a decrease in relative proportion of FoxP3+ Tregs and an increase in relative proportion of CD8+ T cells in the spleen compared to control CIA mice (Figure 3A–B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, B-C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A-B.

claim: Activated CD8+ T cells were increased in the circulation of RA patients compared to otherwise healthy people.
source: This is similar to what was observed in people with RA, as activated CD8+ T cells were increased and Tregs were decreased in the circulation of RA patients compared to otherwise healthy people (Morita et al., 2016; Ramwadhdoebe et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to existing literature on T cells in RA patients.

claim: Tregs were decreased in the circulation of RA patients compared to otherwise healthy people.
source: This is similar to what was observed in people with RA, as activated CD8+ T cells were increased and Tregs were decreased in the circulation of RA patients compared to otherwise healthy people (Morita et al., 2016; Ramwadhdoebe et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to existing literature on T cells in RA patients.

claim: In the ILNs of γHV68-CIA mice, there was a nonsignificant trend of decreased CD8+ and CD4+ T cell relative proportions, indicating potential T cell egress from the ILNs during disease.
source: In the ILNs of γHV68-CIA mice, we observed a nonsignificant trend of decreased CD8+ and CD4+ T cell relative proportions, indicating potential T cell egress from the ILNs during disease, and found that the proportion of regulatory T cells was unchanged between CIA and γHV68-CIA mice (Figure 3A–B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1E–G).
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data showing trends in T cell proportions.

claim: The proportion of regulatory T cells in ILNs was unchanged between CIA and γHV68-CIA mice.
source: In the ILNs of γHV68-CIA mice, we observed a nonsignificant trend of decreased CD8+ and CD4+ T cell relative proportions, indicating potential T cell egress from the ILNs during disease, and found that the proportion of regulatory T cells was unchanged between CIA and γHV68-CIA mice (Figure 3A–B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1E–G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A-B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E-G.

claim: There was a significant increase in relative proportion of CD11c+CD8+ dendritic cells in γHV68-CIA mice compared to CIA.
source: We also observed a significant increase in relative proportion of CD11c+CD8+dendritic cells (DCs) in γHV68-CIA mice compared to CIA (Figure 3—figure supplement 1H–J).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1H-J.

claim: The T cell profile of γHV68-CIA mice is skewed pathogenically, with decreased Tregs and increased cytotoxic T cells.
source: These data show that the T cell profile of γHV68-CIA mice is skewed pathogenically, with decreased Tregs and increased cytotoxic T cells.
evidence: This is a summary of experimental findings from Figure 3.

claim: Both IL17 and IFNγ are involved in RA.
source: Although IL17 has been highly studied due to its predominance in animal models of arthritis, both IL17 and IFNγ are involved in RA (Yamada et al., 2008; Ramwadhdoebe et al., 2016; Shen et al., 2009; Nistala et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to existing literature on cytokines in RA.

claim: In γHV68-CIA, greater numbers of splenic CD8+ and CD4+ T cells express IFNγ compared to CIA alone.
source: As expected from our previous work with γHV68-EAE, we found that in γHV68-CIA, greater numbers of splenic CD8+ and CD4+ T cells express IFNγ compared to CIA alone (Figure 3C–D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C-D.

claim: There is a maintenance of Th17 cells in the spleen, with a similar proportion of CD4+ T cells expressing IL17A in CIA and γHV68-CIA.
source: There is a maintenance of Th17 cells in the spleen, with a similar proportion of CD4+ T cells expressing IL17A in CIA and γHV68-CIA (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: In the ILNs, there was a significant increase in Il17a by RT-qPCR.
source: In the ILNs, we observed a significant increase in Il17a by RT-qPCR (Figure 3E) and a corresponding trend toward more IL17A-expressing CD4+ T cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: In the ILNs, there was a corresponding trend toward more IL17A-expressing CD4+ T cells.
source: In the ILNs, we observed a significant increase in Il17a by RT-qPCR (Figure 3E) and a corresponding trend toward more IL17A-expressing CD4+ T cells.
evidence: This is an observation from experimental data, though not shown in a figure.

claim: The combined Th1 and Th17 profile observed in γHV68-CIA is more reminiscent of what is observed in people with RA than in CIA without γHV68 infection.
source: We propose that the combined Th1 and Th17 profile observed in γHV68-CIA is more reminiscent of what is observed in people with RA than in CIA without γHV68 infection.
evidence: This is a proposal based on comparison of experimental data with known characteristics of RA.

claim: In ACRTA-γHV68, the genes responsible for latency were deleted and a lytic gene, RTA, was constitutively expressed, resulting in clearance of the acute virus by day 14 post-infection.
source: In ACRTA-γHV68, the genes responsible for latency were deleted and a lytic gene, RTA, was constitutively expressed, resulting in clearance of the acute virus by day 14 post-infection (Rickabaugh et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to existing literature on ACRTA-γHV68 characteristics.

claim: ACRTA-γHV68-infected mice did not develop the CIA clinical enhancement that was observed in latently γHV68-infected mice.
source: We found that ACRTA-γHV68-infected mice did not develop the CIA clinical enhancement that we observed in latently γHV68-infected mice, with the clinical course and day of onset resembling that of uninfected CIA mice (Figure 4A–B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A-B.

claim: The clinical course and day of onset in ACRTA-γHV68-infected mice resembled that of uninfected CIA mice.
source: We found that ACRTA-γHV68-infected mice did not develop the CIA clinical enhancement that we observed in latently γHV68-infected mice, with the clinical course and day of onset resembling that of uninfected CIA mice (Figure 4A–B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A-B.

claim: The immunological changes observed in γHV68-CIA mice, when compared to CIA mice, were absent in ACRTA-γHV68 CIA mice.
source: Furthermore, the immunological changes observed in γHV68-CIA mice, when compared to CIA mice, were absent in ACRTA-γHV68 CIA mice.
evidence: This is a summary of experimental findings from Figure 4.

claim: The increase in relative proportion of CD8+ T cells in the spleen was less pronounced in ACRTA-γHV68 CIA compared to γHV68-CIA.
source: The increase in relative proportion of CD8+ T cells in the spleen was less pronounced in ACRTA-γHV68 CIA compared to γHV68-CIA, while there was no change in relative proportion of CD4+ T cells (Figure 4C–D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C-D.

claim: There was no change in relative proportion of CD4+ T cells in the spleen in ACRTA-γHV68 CIA.
source: The increase in relative proportion of CD8+ T cells in the spleen was less pronounced in ACRTA-γHV68 CIA compared to γHV68-CIA, while there was no change in relative proportion of CD4+ T cells (Figure 4C–D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C-D.

claim: In ACRTA-γHV68 CIA mice, there was abolishment of the γHV68-induced upregulation of IFNγ in CD8+ and CD4+ T cells.
source: In ACRTA-γHV68 CIA mice, there was abolishment of the γHV68-induced upregulation of IFNγ in CD8+ and CD4+ T cells, reflecting altered functional capacity and possibly specificity, and no change in IL17A expression by CD4+ T cells (Figure 4E–G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E-G.

claim: In ACRTA-γHV68 CIA mice, there was no change in IL17A expression by CD4+ T cells.
source: In ACRTA-γHV68 CIA mice, there was abolishment of the γHV68-induced upregulation of IFNγ in CD8+ and CD4+ T cells, reflecting altered functional capacity and possibly specificity, and no change in IL17A expression by CD4+ T cells (Figure 4E–G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E-G.

claim: The decrease in relative proportion of splenic Tregs observed in γHV68 CIA mice was not present in ACRTA-γHV68 CIA mice.
source: The decrease in relative proportion of splenic Tregs and CD8+ infiltration into the synovial fluid observed in γHV68 CIA mice was not present in ACRTA-γHV68 CIA mice (Figure 4H–I).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4H-I.

claim: CD8+ infiltration into the synovial fluid observed in γHV68 CIA mice was not present in ACRTA-γHV68 CIA mice.
source: The decrease in relative proportion of splenic Tregs and CD8+ infiltration into the synovial fluid observed in γHV68 CIA mice was not present in ACRTA-γHV68 CIA mice (Figure 4H–I).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4H-I.

claim: ACRTA-γHV68 CIA mice displayed a similar clinical and immunological profile to uninfected CIA mice.
source: Together, these data show that ACRTA-γHV68 CIA mice displayed a similar clinical and immunological profile to uninfected CIA mice.
evidence: This is a summary of experimental findings from Figure 4.

claim: The enhancement of CIA is not due to innate immune stimulation during the acute infection, but rather the latency phase of γHV68 infection is critical for the clinical and immunological exacerbation of CIA.
source: This demonstrates that the enhancement is not due to innate immune stimulation during the acute infection, but, rather, the latency phase of γHV68 infection is critical for the clinical and immunological exacerbation of CIA.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data comparing latent γHV68 and ACRTA-γHV68.

claim: The requirement of γHV68 latency mirrors the RA patient clinical course, wherein patients are infected with EBV years before the onset of disease.
source: The requirement of γHV68 latency mirrors the RA patient clinical course, wherein patients are infected with EBV years before the onset of disease.
evidence: This is an inference connecting experimental findings to human disease characteristics.

claim: CIA induction increased the proportion and total number of ABCs (CD19+CD11c+Tbet+) in the spleen.
source: We found that CIA induction increased the proportion and total number of ABCs (CD19+CD11c+Tbet+) in the spleen, and γHV68-CIA mice had further increased proportions of ABCs in the spleen compared to CIA (Figure 5A–B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A-B.

claim: γHV68-CIA mice had further increased proportions of ABCs in the spleen compared to CIA.
source: We found that CIA induction increased the proportion and total number of ABCs (CD19+CD11c+Tbet+) in the spleen, and γHV68-CIA mice had further increased proportions of ABCs in the spleen compared to CIA (Figure 5A–B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A-B.

claim: The proportion of ABCs in the ILNs was not significantly different between γHV68-CIA and CIA mice.
source: The proportion of ABCs in the ILNs was not significantly different between γHV68-CIA and CIA mice (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The number of ABCs was substantially lower in the ILNs than in the spleen.
source: The number of ABCs was substantially lower in the ILNs than in the spleen, concurring with other studies that found that ABCs primarily reside in the spleen (Johnson et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and citation to existing literature.

claim: ABCs primarily reside in the spleen.
source: The number of ABCs was substantially lower in the ILNs than in the spleen, concurring with other studies that found that ABCs primarily reside in the spleen (Johnson et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to existing literature.

claim: During CIA and γHV68-CIA, there were no differences in the proportions of ABCs between male and female mice.
source: During CIA and γHV68-CIA, we did not observe differences in the proportions of ABCs between male and female mice (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: ABCs in the spleen were phenotypically distinct in γHV68-CIA compared to CIA.
source: We next examined the phenotypic characteristics and found that ABCs in the spleen were phenotypically distinct in γHV68-CIA compared to CIA.
evidence: This is a summary of experimental findings from Figure 5.

claim: Fewer ABCs in the spleens of γHV68-CIA mice expressed IL10.
source: We found that fewer ABCs in the spleens of γHV68-CIA mice expressed IL10, while an increased proportion expressed IFNγ (Figure 5C), indicating that they are skewed toward a pathogenic Th1 phenotype.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: An increased proportion of ABCs in the spleens of γHV68-CIA mice expressed IFNγ.
source: We found that fewer ABCs in the spleens of γHV68-CIA mice expressed IL10, while an increased proportion expressed IFNγ (Figure 5C), indicating that they are skewed toward a pathogenic Th1 phenotype.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: ABCs in γHV68-CIA are skewed toward a pathogenic Th1 phenotype.
source: We found that fewer ABCs in the spleens of γHV68-CIA mice expressed IL10, while an increased proportion expressed IFNγ (Figure 5C), indicating that they are skewed toward a pathogenic Th1 phenotype.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cytokine expression pattern of ABCs.

claim: Fewer splenic ABCs in γHV68-CIA mice expressed inhibitory receptors CTLA4, PDL1, and PD1.
source: Further, fewer splenic ABCs in γHV68-CIA mice expressed inhibitory receptors CTLA4, PDL1, and PD1 (Figure 5D–F), and thus ABCs in CIA displayed a more regulatory phenotype than those in γHV68-CIA mice.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D-F.

claim: ABCs in CIA displayed a more regulatory phenotype than those in γHV68-CIA mice.
source: Further, fewer splenic ABCs in γHV68-CIA mice expressed inhibitory receptors CTLA4, PDL1, and PD1 (Figure 5D–F), and thus ABCs in CIA displayed a more regulatory phenotype than those in γHV68-CIA mice.
evidence: This is an inference based on the expression of inhibitory receptors.

claim: The ABCs in γHV68-CIA mice displayed a more mature phenotype, with fewer IgD+IgM+ naive B cells and increased MHCII expression.
source: Additionally, the ABCs in γHV68-CIA mice displayed a more mature phenotype, with fewer IgD+IgM+ naive B cells and increased MHCII expression, though the expression of memory marker CD27 was unchanged (Figure 5G–I).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5G-I.

claim: The expression of memory marker CD27 on ABCs was unchanged between γHV68-CIA and CIA.
source: Additionally, the ABCs in γHV68-CIA mice displayed a more mature phenotype, with fewer IgD+IgM+ naive B cells and increased MHCII expression, though the expression of memory marker CD27 was unchanged (Figure 5G–I).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5G-I.

claim: ABCs in γHV68-CIA mice are more mature and may have increased antigen presentation capacities but are not primarily a memory subset.
source: These results indicate that ABCs in γHV68-CIA mice are more mature and may have increased antigen presentation capacities but are not primarily a memory subset.
evidence: This is an inference based on the phenotypic characteristics of ABCs.

claim: There were no differences in the expression of CD20, TNFα, CD95 (Fas), nor IDO expression on ABCs between γHV68-CIA and CIA.
source: There were no differences in the expression of CD20, TNFα, CD95 (Fas), nor IDO expression (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D–G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D-G.

claim: ABCs in γHV68-CIA mice display a more pathogenic phenotype than those in CIA, with decreased expression of regulatory cytokine IL10 and inhibitory markers, and increased expression of IFNγ.
source: Collectively, these results indicate that ABCs in γHV68-CIA mice display a more pathogenic phenotype than those in CIA, with decreased expression of regulatory cytokine IL10 and inhibitory markers, and increased expression of IFNγ.
evidence: This is a summary of experimental findings from Figure 5.

claim: The clinical course was unchanged in CIA between Ctrl and KO mice, indicating that ABCs are not contributing to the disease course in CIA.
source: We observed that the clinical course was unchanged in CIA between Ctrl and KO mice, indicating that ABCs are not contributing to the disease course in CIA (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B and inference from the lack of difference.

claim: When induced with CIA, γHV68-infected KO mice did not display the γHV68-exacerbated clinical course compared to γHV68-CIA Ctrl mice, indicating that ABCs are a pathogenic subset in γHV68-CIA.
source: Alternatively, when induced with CIA, γHV68-infected KO mice did not display the γHV68-exacerbated clinical course compared to γHV68-CIA Ctrl mice (Figure 6C), indicating that ABCs are a pathogenic subset in γHV68-CIA.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C and inference from the lack of exacerbation in KO mice.

claim: Without ABCs, γHV68-CIA mice did not display clinical exacerbation, but rather appeared similar to uninfected CIA mice in terms of disease severity and day of onset.
source: Without ABCs, γHV68-CIA mice did not display clinical exacerbation, but rather appeared similar to uninfected CIA mice in terms of disease severity and day of onset (Figure 6B–D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B-D.

claim: The ablation of ABCs does not significantly alter the proportion of CD8, CD4, or Treg populations in the spleen during CIA or γHV68-CIA.
source: We observed that the ablation of ABCs does not significantly alter the proportion of CD8, CD4, or Treg populations in the spleen during CIA or γHV68-CIA, nor the expression of IFNγ or IL17A (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The ablation of ABCs does not significantly alter the expression of IFNγ or IL17A in the spleen during CIA or γHV68-CIA.
source: We observed that the ablation of ABCs does not significantly alter the proportion of CD8, CD4, or Treg populations in the spleen during CIA or γHV68-CIA, nor the expression of IFNγ or IL17A (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: ABCs are a critical pathogenic population in γHV68-CIA.
source: These results indicate that ABCs are a critical pathogenic population in γHV68-CIA though more work is needed to fully elucidate the mechanism by which ABCs are contributing to disease.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data from ABC knockout experiments.

claim: Latent γHV68 exacerbates CIA clinically and immunologically.
source: In this report, we demonstrate that latent γHV68 exacerbates CIA clinically and immunologically, and Tbet+ B cells, known as ABCs, are critical for this exacerbation.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings of the study.

claim: Tbet+ B cells, known as ABCs, are critical for the exacerbation of CIA by latent γHV68.
source: In this report, we demonstrate that latent γHV68 exacerbates CIA clinically and immunologically, and Tbet+ B cells, known as ABCs, are critical for this exacerbation.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings of the study.

claim: Infecting mice with latent γHV68 prior to CIA induction results in an immune course more similar to that of RA patients than CIA alone.
source: Here, we show that infecting mice with latent γHV68 prior to CIA induction results in an immune course more similar to that of RA patients than CIA alone and is a suitable model for examining the contribution of EBV to RA.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on comparison of experimental findings with known characteristics of RA.

claim: The γHV68-CIA model is a suitable model for examining the contribution of EBV to RA.
source: Here, we show that infecting mice with latent γHV68 prior to CIA induction results in an immune course more similar to that of RA patients than CIA alone and is a suitable model for examining the contribution of EBV to RA.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: Elucidating how EBV infection contributes to the development of RA is critical to understanding the underlying pathophysiology of the disease.
source: Elucidating how EBV infection contributes to the development of RA is critical to understanding the underlying pathophysiology of the disease.
evidence: This is a statement about the importance of the research.

claim: There is overlap in etiology and pathophysiology between autoimmune diseases associated with EBV.
source: The overlap in etiology and pathophysiology between these autoimmune diseases may help to explain the cross-efficacy of immunotherapies between MS and RA, including B cell-depletion therapies.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of cross-efficacy of therapies.

claim: The overlap in etiology and pathophysiology between autoimmune diseases may help to explain the cross-efficacy of immunotherapies between MS and RA, including B cell-depletion therapies.
source: The overlap in etiology and pathophysiology between these autoimmune diseases may help to explain the cross-efficacy of immunotherapies between MS and RA, including B cell-depletion therapies.
evidence: This is speculation about the implications of shared disease mechanisms.

claim: In both the γHV68-CIA and γHV68-EAE models, there was an increase in CD8+ T cells at the site of disease and increased expression of IFNγ by cytotoxic and helper T cells.
source: In both the γHV68-CIA and γHV68-EAE models, we observed an increase in CD8+ T cells at the site of disease and increased expression of IFNγ by cytotoxic and helper T cells.
evidence: This is a comparison of findings from the current study with previous work.

claim: Latent gammaherpesvirus infection of mice alters autoimmune disease onset and severity reminiscent of the strong association of latent EBV infection in RA patients.
source: Latent gammaherpesvirus infection of mice clearly alters autoimmune disease onset and severity reminiscent of the strong association of latent EBV infection in RA patients.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental findings and comparison to human disease.

claim: These investigative models will serve to identify common mechanisms in which EBV contributes to multiple autoimmune diseases.
source: As such, these investigative models will serve to identify common mechanisms in which EBV contributes to multiple autoimmune diseases.
evidence: This is speculation about the future utility of the models.

claim: Latent EBV infection modulates the peripheral immune response in a manner that contributes to the development of RA.
source: Due to EBV infection often taking place years before the onset of arthritis, we posit that latent EBV infection modulates the peripheral immune response in a manner that contributes to the development of RA.
evidence: This is speculation based on the temporal relationship between EBV infection and RA onset.

claim: Latently EBV-infected B cells alter, either directly or indirectly, lymphocytes that go on to contribute to disease onset, likely through expanding and activating CD8+ T cells and skewing toward a Th1 response.
source: We suggest that latently EBV-infected B cells alter, either directly or indirectly, lymphocytes that go on to contribute to disease onset, likely through expanding and activating CD8+ T cells and skewing toward a Th1 response.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism based on experimental findings.

claim: CD11c+CD8+ DCs may play a role in priming the pathogenic CD8+ T cell response.
source: CD11c+CD8+ DCs may play a role in priming the pathogenic CD8+ T cell response, as they have been shown to cross-present antigen (den Haan et al., 2000; Schulz and Reis e Sousa, 2002).
evidence: This is speculation based on known functions of CD11c+CD8+ DCs and supported by citations.

claim: CD11c+CD8+ DCs have been shown to cross-present antigen.
source: CD11c+CD8+ DCs may play a role in priming the pathogenic CD8+ T cell response, as they have been shown to cross-present antigen (den Haan et al., 2000; Schulz and Reis e Sousa, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to existing literature.

claim: ABCs are likely critical moderators in driving the heightened Th1 immune response to latent viral infection.
source: By acting as a mediator between infected cells and pathogenic T cells, ABCs are likely critical moderators in driving the heightened Th1 immune response to latent viral infection.
evidence: This is speculation about the role of ABCs based on experimental findings.

claim: ABCs function pathogenically in mouse models of lupus.
source: Accumulating evidence shows that ABCs are expanded in multiple autoimmune diseases and function pathogenically in mouse models of lupus (Rubtsov et al., 2011; Thorarinsdottir et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2019; Claes et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2019; Rakhmanov et al., 2009; Rubtsova et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to existing literature.

claim: Precisely how ABCs are contributing to pathogenicity is unclear.
source: Precisely how ABCs are contributing to pathogenicity is unclear, and ABCs are known to display multiple functional capacities that could contribute to disease.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: In models of SLE, ABCs have been shown to secrete autoantibodies and compromise germinal center responses.
source: In models of SLE, ABCs have been shown to secrete autoantibodies and compromise germinal center responses (Zhang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to existing literature.

claim: ABCs function as excellent antigen-presenting cells.
source: Additionally, ABCs function as excellent antigen-presenting cells (Rubtsov et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to existing literature.

claim: In a model of SLE, the ablation of ABCs decreases activated CD4+ T cells and IFNγ-CD8+ T cells.
source: In a model of SLE, the ablation of ABCs decreases activated CD4+ T cells and IFNγ-CD8+ T cells (Rubtsova et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to existing literature.

claim: ABCs have been shown to secrete regulatory IL10.
source: Alternatively, ABCs have been shown to secrete regulatory IL10 (Rubtsov et al., 2011; Hao et al., 2011), suggesting that a portion of the ABC population, in some individuals or contexts, could function in a protective manner.
evidence: This is supported by citations to existing literature.

claim: A portion of the ABC population, in some individuals or contexts, could function in a protective manner.
source: Alternatively, ABCs have been shown to secrete regulatory IL10 (Rubtsov et al., 2011; Hao et al., 2011), suggesting that a portion of the ABC population, in some individuals or contexts, could function in a protective manner.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation that ABCs can secrete IL10.

claim: RA patients who experience a relapse following B cell-depletion therapy are more likely to display a reconstitution profile with increased numbers of memory B cells.
source: RA patients who experience a relapse following B cell-depletion therapy are more likely to display a reconstitution profile with increased numbers of memory B cells (Leandro et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to existing literature.

claim: ABCs are pathogenic in a genetic model of SLE without the presence of a virus.
source: It is intriguing that ABCs are pathogenic in a genetic model of SLE without the presence of a virus (Rubtsova et al., 2017), though we observe that latent γHV68 is necessary for the pathogenicity of ABCs in CIA.
evidence: This is supported by citation to existing literature.

claim: Latent γHV68 is necessary for the pathogenicity of ABCs in CIA.
source: It is intriguing that ABCs are pathogenic in a genetic model of SLE without the presence of a virus (Rubtsova et al., 2017), though we observe that latent γHV68 is necessary for the pathogenicity of ABCs in CIA.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental findings from ABC knockout experiments.

claim: ABCs may be contributing to disease through various mechanisms or different contexts can prime ABCs for pathogenicity.
source: This discrepancy indicates that ABCs may be contributing to disease through various mechanisms or that different contexts can prime ABCs for pathogenicity.
evidence: This is speculation about the implications of differences between SLE and CIA models.

claim: ABCs are critical for an effective anti-influenza response.
source: The role of ABCs in controlling viral infections is an ongoing topic of study, with multiple papers recently providing compelling evidence that ABCs are critical for an effective anti-influenza response (Johnson et al., 2020) and are required to control LCMV infection (Barnett et al., 2016), in part through their secretion of antiviral IgG2a.
evidence: This is supported by citation to existing literature.

claim: ABCs are required to control LCMV infection, in part through their secretion of antiviral IgG2a.
source: The role of ABCs in controlling viral infections is an ongoing topic of study, with multiple papers recently providing compelling evidence that ABCs are critical for an effective anti-influenza response (Johnson et al., 2020) and are required to control LCMV infection (Barnett et al., 2016), in part through their secretion of antiviral IgG2a.
evidence: This is supported by citation to existing literature.

claim: An in vivo model that recapitulates the temporal and systemic immunological aspects of the relationship between EBV and RA is critical.
source: An in vivo model that recapitulates the temporal and systemic immunological aspects of the relationship between EBV and RA is critical.
evidence: This is a statement about the need for appropriate models.

claim: Clearance of the acute γHV68 virus and establishment of latency have previously been shown by plaque assay on spleens collected 35 days post-infection.
source: Clearance of the acute virus and establishment of latency have previously been shown by plaque assay on spleens collected 35 days post-infection (Casiraghi et al., 2012; Barton et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to existing literature.

claim: Latent γHV68-infected mice (without CIA) did not display any signs of disease.
source: As expected, latent γHV68-infected mice (without CIA) did not display any signs of disease (Figure 1A–B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A-B.

claim: IFNγ-producing T cells are present in the synovium of RA patients.
source: Together, these results indicate that IFNγ-producing T cells were preferentially infiltrating the synovium in our model of γHV68-CIA, which is consistent with what was observed in the synovium of RA patients (Yamada et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to existing literature on RA.
